newsitem.title: UK: Physical copper trade patchy, premiums fluctuate.
newsitem.headline: Physical copper trade patchy, premiums fluctuate.

text.p: Business in Europe's physical copper market is beginning to pick up, following the end-1996 holiday hiatus, although premium and discount levels were proving difficult to pin down, traders said.
This was mostly because of the wide backwardation currently prevailing on the London Metal Exchange (LME), which means that spot levels will vary widely.

The backwardation has had the affect of attracting some metal to the market, while the shortage of scrap and Russian off-grade material, which was acute in the last quarter, has eased to some extent now, they said.
"Business is not too bad at the moment...At the start of January there was the odd parcel in Europe that needed to be concluded," one trader said.

However, there appears to be a wide variance in spot premium ideas, with rates fluctuating widely depending on whether spot covering needs to be done or if metal is being sold against the backwardation, which is currently at $240, basis cash/threes LME.
For one month forward copper, premium/discount levels are more consistent, and appear to be holding at steady levels, others said.
Whereas, Grade A in Rotterdam is around $30/35 over LME, slightly forward there have been offers of prompt at levels nearer $80, some said.
Another factor behind the wide difference in spot European quotes is the well-documented movement of metal from Europe to the Far East due to the arbitrage opportunities that arose last autumn.
"A lot of metal went out to the Far East, and a lot did not arrive in Europe because of producer swaps," one noted.
Meanwhile, spot Russian offgrade copper is anywhere between premiums over $30 in some instances for good quality cathode to discounts near $30.
"There is a bit more Russian around, as well as scrap. Prices have picked up since the last quarter of 1996, so there is more scrap coming into the system," another trader said.
Broker Merrill Lynch, in its recent bi-weekly report, said that scrap supplies in the West are more plentiful because of higher LME prices.
"When prices fall back to, say, 85 cents/lb that is when scrap should start to dry up again," the broker said. Current LME cash prices are around $2,205 a tonne, or $1.13 cents/lb.
